cards.note: If you see a Street View car with a slightly rusted black truck bed, you know you're in American Samoa.

Andorra has a lot of these distinct stone buildings, visible almost everywhere in the country.

These buildings can also be found near Andorra, in the French and Spanish Pyrenees.
This double-rounded concrete pole connected by a concrete ring is almost exclusive to Argentina. Similar ones can occasionally be found in Bolivia, but the landscape will be vastly different.
If you see black-and-white highway markers, you're in Argentina.

If you find yourself in a flat, desolate, treeless, sparsely populated area with a visible black back of the Google car, you're likely in Argentina.

(Jordan might resemble this landscape for new players, and it also has a black back on the car, so be aware of that.)

(Only other countries in South America with car like that are: Peru and Uruguay)
Old license plates in Argentina have a black dot in the middle of a white plate, which is easy to spot. New license plates are fully white with a blue line at the top, similar to those in Brazil.

Australian bollards are white with a red reflector on the front and grey on the back.

Turkish bollards are similar but lack a back reflector. If unsure, check the sun position, landscape, or vegetation.
Give-way signs in Australia have a white border and black text, while in New Zealand, they have red text.
The iconic Stobie pole, made of steel and concrete, is specific to South Australia.(A few thousand of these poles can be found in other states, most notably Tasmania - super rare)
Yellow signposts are specific to Western Australia.

Austria's bollards are white with a black top and dark red or grey reflectors, often featuring a nipple-shaped black cap and sometimes a snow pole.

Slovenia’s bollards are similar but always have a white back reflector, whereas in Austria, white reflectors are rare but possible.

The Bengali script features a continuous horizontal line at the top of each word. It resembles Devanagari (Hindi) but can be recognized by the many letters with triangular shapes. Bengali is an official language in Bangladesh and parts of eastern India(but coverage there is taken with "shit cam")
Belgian license plates should have a red tint visible through the blur because they use red text on a white license plate.
If you see a black Street View car with the entire front side of the vehicle visible, you're in Bermuda.
Traditional Bhutanese architecture is very distinct. Most houses feature tin roofs and wooden painted frames, giving them a unique look.
License plates in Bhutan are almost always red and are easily visible on vehicles.
Bhutan commonly uses stone blocks as safety barriers on winding rural roads. These blocks are very common and are one of the best ways to recognize rural roads in Bhutan.
Many wooden utility poles, particularly in the eastern parts of Bolivia are noticeably curvy and appear to be made from locally sourced tree trunks.

A dry, flat landscape with African vegetation, usually a bit away from the road, is a good clue for Botswana and becomes quite distinct after seeing it couple times. You can confirm it's Botswana by the white back of the Google car, driving on the left, yellow outer lines, and the sun in the north.

The only other countries in Africa with that combination are:

  • Eswatini & Lesotho (but they will be hilly)
  • South Africa (though this is rare, as most of the coverage now is with blue back of the google car).
If the landscape and vegetation make it look like you're in South America and you see signs with a black back, you're most likely in Brazil.
Blue Fortlev water tanks are often seen on Brazilian roofs.

These distinct trees, called Paraná pines, have long horizontal branches with leaves only at the end. They grow mainly in the southern Brazilian states of Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul.

The most common poles in Brazil resemble a ladder at the bottom. They are rectangular, with long segments at the base and small holes near the top. Chilean poles look similar but have 1–2 larger sections at the bottom instead of 3+ like Brazilian poles.

You might also find rounded concrete or wooden poles in Brazil, but they are less common and can be used for region-guessing within the country.

A blue road marker with the road number at the top and the kilometer at the bottom is common in Brazil. Sometimes, the first two letters of the road number can tell you the state you're in (unless it starts with "BR").

(If you zoom out on the map where you can guess and look at Brazil, you’ll see short two-letter abbreviations for Brazilian states.)
This style of pole top, featuring 3 large, alternating insulators shaped like upward-facing hooks, is a good clue for Bulgaria. This pole top is likely unique to the country.

Most poles in Bulgaria have small, alternating hook-shaped insulators, which can also be found in other countries (mostly on wooden poles, like Latvia, North Macedonia, and a few others). However, if you see them on a concrete pole, you're most likely in Bulgaria. Try using other clues to confirm.
Town entry signs in Bulgaria have a simple white design and use both the Cyrillic and Latin alphabets. Like directional signs, the two lines of text are clear and visible even from a distance.
In Cambodia, wooden houses on stilts are very common. The walls are often made of vertical planks, and many homes have double or triple roofs.

Cambodia for the most part uses two types of poles: a concrete ladder (or "waffle") pole, where the compartments are not holes but just indents, and a round concrete pole with holes along its whole length and a peculiar pattern in the top part. You can also rarely find wooden and thin metal poles.

Alberta has a unique black and white bollard that is often found at intersections. It has a cylindrical shape and two black bands that wrap all the way around. It is one of the most useful Canadian bollards to learn because it appears so frequently.
This diamond-shaped T-intersection "checkboard" sign is unique to Canada.
Canadian speed limit signs have the word "Maximum," while U.S. signs use "Speed Limit."
You can find these diamond-shaped markers on the sides of the roads in Ontario. The colours can vary.
Ontario speed limit signs may feature a black section at the bottom, with the words "km/h" or "begins" written in white.
Stop signs with the word ‘Arret’ are unique to Quebec in Canada.
Within the Americas, all-yellow road lines are essentially unique to Chile. These lines are typically seen in National Parks or areas of high snowfall, as Chile usually uses all-white lines.
Chile signs commonly have those empty slots at the top of signposts.

Chile uses square concrete poles with an indent on both sides. They are somewhat similar to Brazilian poles, however have fewer horizontal supports in the indent. The upper part typically has small pinholes.
If you see a Street View car with only the bed of a silver pickup truck visible, you know you're on Christmas Island.

Signposts in Colombia are made of white thin metal and have a distinct cross on the back.

In the photo, green checkmarks show the "real" Colombian cross, and red X's show the ones that aren't right.

In South America, yellow license plates are almost exclusive to Colombia. Commercial vehicles in Colombia may have white plates.

  • Images and descriptions courtesy of Plonkit.net

Croatian bollards are white with a black rectangle and a red or white reflector. From the top, they are shaped like a triangle. Hungarian bollards are similar, but the black part with the reflector is positioned further from the top.

This black Street View car with a roof rack is unique to Curaçao.

It also has white sticker on front left/back right of roof rack.
Bollards in Czechia have orange double reflectors on the front and a single white reflector on the back, with rarer blue and red variants. The same design is also found in Slovakia.

Denmark's bollards are white with a yellow reflector and a distinctive dark orange stripe at the top.

Belgium's bollards are similar but have a rectangular reflector and no orange stripe at the top.
This signpost, where the pipe frame is bent around the sign, is unique to Denmark.
Most Danish street names end in "vej," which means "street" in Danish. Street signs typically have a blue background with white text.

A Street View car with a white front and a roof rack filled with thick black rubber stripes is unique to the Dominican Republic. Only the capital Santo Domingo and the Northern city of Santiago de los Caballeros are covered.

With this landscape - similar cars can be found in Guatemala and Curaçao, but they lack the thick black stripes.

Ecuador is one of the countries in South America that uses bollards extensively, making them quite common in the country. There are two main types of bollards:

  • A round bollard with two red stripes
  • A flat bollard with two red reflectors on black

While other types of bollards can be found, they almost always follow the same color scheme and style.

Round bollards with a rectangular reflector on the front and two circular reflectors on the back, which can be either white or orange, are common. Latvia's bollards might look similar, but they have a "half-circle" or flat curved shape, and sometimes feature numbers on them.

  • Baltic/Nordic bollard infographic
In Estonia, the words for street and road are "tänav" and "tee," respectively. If you see street signs ending in "tee" or "tn" (with "tänav" often abbreviated as 'tn'), you know you're in Estonia.
In Estonia, the words for street and road are "tänav" and "tee," respectively. If you see street signs ending in "tee" or "tn" (with "tänav" often abbreviated as 'tn'), you know you're in Estonia.

Eswatini’s landscape is characterized by green, wooded hills and tall golden grass. Poles are made of dark brown wood and have a simple design, with insulators mostly mounted on the side.

You can confirm it's Eswatini by the white back of the Google car, driving on the left, yellow outer lines, and the sun in the north. The only other countries in Africa with that combination are:

  • Lesotho (which has bare, treeless mountains)
  • Botswana (which is super flat)
  • South Africa (though this is rare, as most of the coverage now is with blue back of the google car).
Street signs in Finland typically have a white background with black text, and most street names end in "tie."
Small blue rectangular markings on utility poles are unique to France. They are often referred to as ‘stickers’ by the community, but are actually small plates.

The French bollard is extremely recognizable and appears very often. It is a round white post with a pointed top and a reflector band going all the way around. The band can be grey or red. Some rare variations have a fully red top. A bollard that is commonly found in Scotland looks similar, but has a blunt top instead of a pointed one.

In France, these concrete ladder poles are pretty common. They're called "ladder" poles because of its similarity to the steps of a ladder.

NOTE: Spain can have the same poles, try using landscape or language to tell them apart.
These middle road lines, where each dash consists of two offset blocks, are unique to France. They are not extremely common, but when you see them, you can safely guess France.
The French word for street is “rue”. Street signs with "rue" can also be found in Belgium.

Germany uses these black and white bollards, with white and light-grey reflectors. The reflector will be orange on bollards next to intersections. They sometimes have plates containing the road number, and potentially other useful information. Many bollards also feature blue attachments on the side.

NOTE: Many European countries have similar bollards, however most will have different coloured reflectors. Luxembourg uses almost identical bollards, but they have 3 bolts instead of 2 on the reflector.

All regular road coverage in Ghana features a unique Google car with a visible roof rack and a piece of black tape on the right end of the front bar. The hood is usually visible, displaying a Street View car wrapping with a red rectangle and other distinctive elements.
These distinctive poletops, which have a metal frame shaped vaguely like a harp, are unique to Greece.

Poles in Greece are usually wooden and often will have this lamp with round shade above the light bulb. (You can sometimes find similar lamps in Serbia/North Macedonia so use other clues to confirm it's Greece)

The Greek language features a unique alphabet not used in any other language. It shares similarities with both the latin and cyrillic alphabet, however the lower case letters generally have softer shapes than the cyrillic letters.

Coverage in Greenland was taken with many different vehicles. Architecture and landscape look very similar all over Greenland but it's hard to put it in words but it's pretty recognizable that's why I included it in this map.

The entire Google car is blurred, however an antenna at the front right and a tiny part of the roof rack can be seen. You can confuse it with:

  • Puerto Rico(Cars there won't have front plates, signs will be Spanish).
  • Northern Mariana Islands(Antenna there will be noticeably closer to the camera but as long you will go Guam/NMI and not Puerto Rico you will get good score.

This gray Street View car with a visible roof rack and mirrors is unique to Guatemala. Don’t confuse it with the Dominican Republic car, which has black stripes on the roof rack, or the Curaçao car, which has a black front. A similar car is found in Laos, so always check the surroundings before making a guess.

Hungarian bollards are black-and-white, wedge-shaped, and typically have a red reflector at the front, and a white reflector at the back. (Croatian bollards are similar but the black part with reflector is closer to the top).

Note: Can appear in slovakia

Concrete holey poles with medium-sized holes going all the way to the bottom are common. They are similar to those in Poland and Romania, but Polish poles have holes that don't go all the way to the top or bottom, and Romanian poles are usually wider and painted white at the bottom.
These green kilometre markers can be seen along most Hungarian roads.
Iceland's yellow bollards with a white reflector are unique and extremely common, found on almost every section of rural road across the country.
Motorcycles in Indonesia have front licence plates, as opposed to other south-east Asian countries which do not.

Indonesian licence plates are black with white letters. The letters usually appear as three white sections through the blur.

Commercial vehicles use yellow licence plates.

Plates in newer coverage can be white too.

NOTE: Malaysian licence plates are also black, but generally have two white sections.
On the Lesser Sunda Islands (“Nusas”), you can find poles with an extra long support on the pole top. Sometimes, two supports can be present.
Many of the steel poles in Indonesia are painted black, and often feature the Indonesian flag colours on them (red and white).
Yellow dashed lines like this are super common in Ireland. You can find sometimes similar lines in New Zealand so if you are not sure use other clues like landscape/vegetation etc.

cards.a: Isle Of Man - Red strip license plate
cards.note: If you feel like you're in the UK or Ireland but notice a red strip on the license plates, you're in the Isle of Man.
If you see cars with yellow front and back license plates in the Middle East, you are in Israel.
Italian bollards are triangular in shape, white with a black top, and feature a red front and a white rear reflector. Albania and San Marino use the same bollards.

A short license plate with a double blue strip on the front and a long plate with a double blue strip on the back is unique to Italy. Similar long plates with a double blue strip can be found in Albania and France, but the front plates won’t be short.
This infrastructural arrow informs drivers of where the shoulder line is when under snow, and is located almost exclusively in Hokkaido(You can find similar rarely in northern prefectures of Japan)

All the coverage taken in Japan is low-cam, the only two other countries with low-cam is Sri Lanka and Switzerland but they look different. You can recognize lowcam because of wide blur of the street view car and lower vantage point compared to normal camera.

While driving on the right side, yellow outer lines with white middle lines are commonly found in Jordan, Israel, and the UAE. The black back of the Google car without an antenna can help confirm you’re in Jordan 100%.
In some of the Kenya coverage, you will be followed by a grey Toyota SUV.

If you see a snorkel on the Google car, you’re in Kenya.

However, the car is sometimes seen without it, so don’t rule out Kenya if the snorkel isn’t visible.

Kyrgyzstan can be recognized by the silver Google car with four visible bars. Coverage was done during winter, so trees often lack leaves, the landscape appears drab, and snow is visible in many areas.

If you are in South East Asia with this roof-rack car you gonna be in one of 4 cities in Laos: Vang Vieng, Luang Prabang, Savannakhet, and Pakse.

Note: You can find similar car in Guatemala so look around before making a guess.

Half-circle/flat curved shape bollards with a rectangular reflector on the front and two circular reflectors on the back are common. The reflectors can be white or orange, and sometimes these bollards have numbers on them.

Estonian bollards might look similar, but they have a rounded shape and will never have numbers on them.
The Latvian word for street is "iela." This word is unique to Latvian, so if you see a street sign with it, you can be sure you're in Latvia.

One of the best ways to identify Lesotho is by its characteristic ‘Lesotho mountains.’ These mountains are bare and treeless, often with tabletop-like shapes and recognizable horizontal rocky ridgelines.

You can confirm it's Lesotho by the white back of the Google car, driving on the left, yellow outer lines, and the sun in the north. The only other countries in Africa with that combination are:

Eswatini (the hills there have trees and usually tall golden grass around) Botswana (which is super flat) South Africa (though this is rare, as most of the coverage now uses the blue back of the Google car).
Lithuanian bollards are wedge-shaped with rectangular reflectors: an orange one on the front and a white one on the back.

The Lithuanian word for street is "gatvė," often abbreviated as "g." on street signs. If you see a street sign ending in "g.," you're likely in Lithuania.

This word is almost entirely unique to Lithuanian, though very rarely, you might see "gatve" (abbreviated as "gat.") in the Latvian capital, Riga.

Bollards in Luxembourg are black and white, wedge-shaped, and feature grey reflectors. Some have a distinctive indent in the lower half.

They look very similar to German bollards, with the main difference being that the reflectors on German bollards are attached with two bolts, while those in Luxembourg have three.

Luxembourg uses long yellow plates with a blue strip on the left. Since Luxembourg is a small country, foreign cars with white plates are somewhat common.

There are only a few other European countries that use yellow plates for private vehicles:

  • The Netherlands has yellow plates front and rear.
  • The UK has yellow rear plates.(driving left in UK)
  • Some pre-2009 French cars have yellow rear plates.
  • Danish commercial vehicles have yellow plates front and rear.

Electricity poles in mainland Malaysia often have black stickers on them, which can have different designs but are always black with white text and sometimes other elements. These stickers are quite distinct, so if it looks like you're in Southeast Asia, it's worth checking the poles for them.
This is a typical Malaysian directional sign. Green background and hexagonal yellow highway shields are unique to Malaysia.
Malaysia frequently uses double white center lines on its two-lane roads, making it the only Southeast Asian country to do so.

Malaysian licence plates are black and generally have two white sections. These are visible even when blurred.

NOTE: Indonesian licence plates are also black, but they will have three white sections.
Thin metal poles with two parallel pole tops are exclusive to the Sabah region of Borneo.
Berhenti stop signs are exclusive to Malaysia.
These thick yellow bars are also almost exclusive to Malaysia. NOTE: You can very rarely see similar patterns in Hong Kong.

If you see a license plate with a blue strip while driving left with this climate/landscape, you know you're in Malta. If you can't see the driving direction, use other clues like limestone rock walls to recognize Malta.
These small, cylindrical white bollards with a black base are unique to Mexico. A yellow reflector is sometimes seen, as well as a flat version.
Mexican kilometer markers are black-rimmed white signs mounted at hip height, featuring the 'km' text and the kilometer number, both in black, arranged vertically.

Most utility poles in Mexico are made of CONCRETE and have an octagonal shape. Sometimes you can find them in Colombia so use different clues to make your guess.

If you see METAL octagonal pole you most likely will be in Philiphines.
In Mexico, arrows on signs are noticeably thick compared to other countries in the Americas.

Gen4 Mongolia coverage was taken with two unique pickup trucks:

-White-Blue themed pickup truck mostly found only in Capital

-Pickup truck with a tent on top
The Street View car with a tent on top is unique to Mongolia. While Mongolia has other unique Google cars, this is the most common one.

Namibia is the newest African country with coverage featuring the white pickup truck.

The landscape is similar to Botswana—flat and dry. Roads typically have yellow outer lines, and driving is on the left side.

Note: You may not always be on main roads with outer yellow lines. In such cases, it can resemble some parts of Kenya, which also drives on the left and sometimes features the white pickup truck.

If you see yellow license plates on both the front and back in Europe with a super flat landscape, it’s likely the Netherlands. Luxembourg also uses all-yellow plates but is much hillier. Denmark may have yellow plates for commercial vehicles, so use other clues like architecture, bike lanes, and surroundings to confirm it’s the Netherlands.
New Zealand has a unique white bollard with a red strip that wraps around the entire back and part of the front.
Give-way signs in New Zealand have a white border and red text, while in Australia, give-way signs use black text.
In Nigeria, Street View coverage often includes a police escort car visible "behind" the Street View car. However, it may sometimes be missing, so don’t rule out Nigeria if you don’t see it.

The entire Google car is blurred, but an antenna at the front right can still be seen. It will feel noticeably closer to the car than in other countries with a similar car.

You can confuse it with:

  • Puerto Rico(Cars there won't have front plates, signs will be Spanish).
  • Guam (You should be able to see little part of roof rack but as long you will guess NMI or Guam and not Peurto Rico you will get good points)

If you see long dashed outer lines, you'll know it's Norway. You can find similar dashed lines with the same climate in Sweden, but they will be half the length, and Finland uses full outer lines.

(N)orway for normal, (S)weden for short, and (F)inland for full.
Many larger roads in Norway have solid outer lines and yellow middle lines. The yellow lines have a distinct tinge of orange, making them easily recognizable.

Black-and-yellow stripes on guardrails are common throughout Peru. Similar striped guardrails can also be found in Bolivia, but to differentiate them, check the outer stripe. Peru uses a black stripe, while Bolivia features a yellow one.
Signs with concrete blocks at the bottom are unique to Peru in South America.
Black-and-white signposts like this are only found in Peru in South America. (If the signpost is inside a city, take this rule with a grain of salt, as you can rarely find them in other countries.)

If you're in Southeast Asia and see concrete roads, you're most likely in the Philippines, Thailand, or, much more rarely, Indonesia. If you're driving on the right side, it will be the Philippines, while driving on the left side indicates Thailand or Indonesia.

Octagonal metal poles are quite common in the Philippines.

NOTE: They can sometimes be found in Bangladesh and some parts of Malaysia as well.
Tuktuks and Trikes are an extremely common sight in the Philippines. In many areas, they are more common than cars.

Center lines in the Philippines can be white or a (usually slightly orange-tinted) yellow. The combination of the two colors, which you can also often get, is not really a thing anywhere else in Southeast Asia and as such is a good indicator for the Philippines.

Polish bollards feature a red strip that wraps around the entire bollard, with a red reflector on the front (sometimes hard to see) and a white reflector on the back. They may also have numbers on them. (from Plonkit)
Holey poles with smaller holes are common in Poland. Similar poles can be found in Hungary and Romania, but in Poland, the holes don't extend all the way to the bottom or the top.
Polish entering town signs have green background and white text with distinct font.
Old Portuguese license plates have a yellow strip on the right side. New plates follow the standard EU design without the yellow strip.
Hunting signs with a red and white color scheme are commonly seen in rural areas of Portugal. They can be either diamond-shaped or rectangular.
Concrete ladder poles with very tall ladder steps are common in Portugal. Each step often has a small see-through hole.

The Portuguese word for street is ‘Rua’.

NOTE: In Galician, the word for road is ‘Rúa’, with an accent on the ‘u’.

Qatar's landscape is predominantly desert, with arid, mostly flat expanses of sand as far as the eye can see. You will often not see many trees or other greenery.

The Google car will usually be blurred, with only the antenna on the left and a sliver of the car visible. Sometimes the entire white pickup truck can be visible.

You might occasionally confuse it with the UAE or Oman pickup truck coverage, but in those countries, the antenna on the pickup car will be in the middle.

Réunion's Street View car features visible side mirrors, a roof rack, and black tape at the end of the rear right bar.

Don’t confuse this with the Ghana car, which has tape on the front right bar.

Concrete holey poles with wide holes and usually painted white at the bottom are common in Romania. They are similar to poles in Poland and Hungary, but Polish poles have smaller holes that don’t go all the way to the bottom or top, and Hungarian poles typically have smaller holes as well.

Within Europe, those red/blue/white KM markers are unique to Romania, the color representing the color the road will show up on the map.

How to use:

On the side is the road number and usually on the front are two cities, the first one is the closest largest city and the second one is the closest town.
Near intersections in Russia you will commonly see a very large number of bollards.

White signposts painted black at the bottom are very common in both Russia and Kazakhstan. However, Kazakhstan's entire coverage was done with a pickup truck, making it easy to rule out, indicating you're in Russia.

This unique very thin type of bollard that is attached to a stick is almost exclusively found in eastern part of Russia (east of Omsk +/-). Russia has a lot more different designs of bollards that you can find anywhere(even in eastern part)
Blue license plates in Africa are unique to Senegal, sometimes you might find license plates that looks like standard europe license plate.
Senegal used to be French colony so you will see similar ladder poles/bollards/lines that you would normally find in France.
Serbian bollards might look like Austria/Slovenia bollards but reflector will be always off-center. They have couple other designs but reflector will be always off-center.
Warnings are often written on the road in large letters, such as the famous “HUMP AHEAD”.
All street name signs in Singapore follow this unique format. They are green, with rounded edges and a distinct white font.
Slovakian bollards have orange double reflectors on the front and a single white reflector on the back, with rarer blue and red variants. The same design is also found in Czechia.

Slovenian bollards are white with a black top, featuring a bright red reflector on the front and a white reflector on the back.

Austria uses similar bollards, but the back reflector is usually black rather than white.

The most common type of pole in South Africa features 1 to 5 horizontal bars with thin white insulators that resemble rows of birds, which is why they are referred to as “bird poles” in the community.

In South Africa, most paved roads have single yellow outer lines and white center lines. This can be used to differentiate from Australia which has only white lines and never single yellow lines.

REMEMBER:

  • The Middle East can also have single yellow outer lines, so use driving side to tell them apart (South Africa drives left)
  • Botswana, Eswatini and Lesotho also use single yellow outer lines (but they usually have a white car)
Korean script is highly distinctive, featuring a combination of circular shapes and blocky, straight-line characters.

Black and yellow diagonal stripes on poles are common in South Korea. You might confuse them with Taiwanese ones, but in South Korea, the stripes never go all the way to the bottom, while the ones in Taiwan usually do and have more of an orange tint to them.
Standard Spanish bollards have a yellow-orange reflector on the front and two white dots on the back, though the back can sometimes be blank. They are typically hollow.

In Spain, these concrete ladder poles can be found amongst other types. They're called "ladder" poles because of its similarity to the steps of a ladder.

NOTE: France can have the same poles, try using landscape or language to tell them apart.

In rural areas of Spain, you will often find no hunting signs. There are two versions, both unique to Spain. One is a simple white sign with text starting with "coto" and ending in "caza." The other has a diagonally divided black and white background.

Spanish pedestrian crossing signs have 8 stripes. This is the highest number of stripes in Europe, and almost unique to Spain.

NOTE: The only other European country with 8 stripes is Andorra.

Spain has distinct road markers, easy to recognize being usually square and having colourful borders. The code on top is the number of the road.

NOTE:: The letter codes before the road number on these markers are often an important region-specific clue, check plonkit for all the code regions.

Spain has yellow reflectors on rounded A-type guardrails.

NOTE: Belgium, Andorra and Gibraltar also have yellow reflectors. For a good overview of European guardrails, see this infographic.

Sri Lanka typically uses concrete utility poles. Two pole types are common and distinctive:

  • Square poles with small pinholes in the sides. These pinholes are limited to the top part of the pole.
  • Poles with large see-through holes in the lower half of the pole (“holey poles“). These poles are unique to Sri Lanka.

They also commonly have those 3 big insulators on top of the pole shown on the second image.

NOTE: The square poles with small pinholes can look very similar to those found in Thailand. However, in Thailand the pinholes extend all the way to the bottom of the pole.

In most Generation 3 Sri Lanka coverage, you will be able to see the front of the Google car partially through the blur. It appears as blue-white-red patches, reminiscent of the French flag, with the red patch usually being the most visually distinct.

If you feel like you're in one of the Nordic countries and see short dashed outer lines, you're likely in Sweden. Norway uses long dashed outer lines, and Finland uses full lines. (N)orway for normal, (S)weden for short, and (F)inland for full).

Warning: Many countries in Europe might also use short or medium dashed outer lines, so be cautious.

All the coverage in Switzerland is taken with a low-cam. The only other two countries with low-cam are Japan and Sri Lanka, but they look different.

You can recognize low-cam by the wide blur of the Street View car and the lower vantage point compared to the normal camera.

Black and yellow diagonal stripes on poles are common. You might confuse them with South Korea's, but in Taiwan, they are usually longer, extend all the way to the bottom of the pole, and have an orange tint to them.

If you're in Southeast Asia and see concrete roads, you're most likely in the Philippines, Thailand, or, much much more rarely, Indonesia. If you're driving on the right side, it will be the Philippines, while driving on the left side indicates Thailand or Indonesia.

Square poles with small holes running from bottom to top are distinctive to Thailand. In Sri Lanka, similar poles exist, but the holes are limited to the top part of the pole.

Note: You can find same poles in Laos(but Laos drives right and most cities coverage is done with google car with roofrack)

Signposts in Thailand are square and bulky in shape, usually white, and often have the bottom painted black.

NOTE: In Southeast Asia, this design is unique to Thailand.

A light green Toyota or dark green Mazda was escorting the Google car through most of Tunisia coverage, and if you look behind, you can almost always see them. Sometimes you won’t see it, so don’t rule out Tunisia if you can't spot the escort car.

Turkish bollards are white and rectangular with a red reflector on the front, making them quite unique. Similar bollards exist in Romania but are very rare. Australian bollards typically have a reflector on the back and a slightly different design(also they drive left in Australia/NZ comparing it to Turkey)
All stop signs in Turkey feature the text "DUR," making them unique to the country. No other country uses this stop sign.
Uganda's unique Google car is white with visible square mirrors, and its coverage is limited to Kampala. Some national parks in Uganda are covered with different cars, but these are quite rare.
A red Google car, with or without an antenna, in Generation 3 and on crappy roads is always Ukraine. However, the car may not always be visible, so don’t rule out Ukraine if you don’t see it.
If you have vibes/other clues that you are in the middle east and you have silver car in Gen3 that means you can only be in UAE.
In the UK, license plates are white on the front and yellow on the back. In Ireland, both the front and back plates are white.

These middle lines, that consist of long dashes with cat’s eyes (reflectors) in the gaps between the dashes, are a good clue for the UK.

Note: You can find it rarely in Ireland.
Utility poles with 3 yellow stripes are most commonly found in California.

cards.a: United States - No passing zone sign
cards.note: Yellow triangular signs with the text "No Passing Zone" are unique to the United States.
U.S. speed limit signs feature the text "Speed Limit," while Canadian signs use the text "Maximum."

In a lot of Uruguay coverage, the camera quality is somewhat smudgy and you will see black back of the google car. You will also commonly see thick white wooden signposts, which are typically painted white. They often have up to four rectangular notches at the back of the post.

Uruguay uses a handful of different utility poles. One very common and useful one are the so-called trident poles, which get their name from their distinctive pole tops with three insulators that point upwards.

NOTE: These trident poles are not found in neighbouring Argentina and Brazil.
Uruguay often has these triple road lines, that consist of double yellow roadlines with white dashes in between. This is a design not seen anywhere else in the Americas.

cards.a: Uruguay - White bollards and stone barriers
cards.note: These white bollards, with one side often painted yellow, and stone barriers, are specific to Uruguay.

cards.a: US Virgin Islands - USV unique car
cards.note: Car coverage on the islands will have a large, visible street view car, which will either be red or white.(Don't confuse it with Bermuda google car which is full black)
The most common bollard type is a small square concrete bollard that is painted white with a red top.
Holey poles, with holes either only on the lower half or almost all the way to the top, are common in Vietnam.
Vietnam uses red-and-white striped signposts, and occasionally red-and-yellow ones.
